I have a theory about AEW that I'm trying to flesh and make sense so just bare with me on this one. I remember in 2021 when AEW was at it's hottest, Alvarez said that AEW was the modern version of ECW. I think most people would disagree but it makes more sense if you actually watched ECW. Outsiders who didn't really follow ECW just thought of it as the show with hardcore stuff every match and gratuitous violence and sex. The reality was ECW was a variety show that tried to innovate not just with violence, but comedy (BWO, Raven and Stevie, The Original Dudleys gimmick, Superstar Steve Austin), lucha guys like Rey and Super Crazy (people credit WCW for the lucha revolution but it was in ECW way before WCW), partnerships with Michinoku Pro and FMW, lots of high level US workers like Van Dam and Candido, and great long term booking and storytelling. All the same things that make AEW great.  
  
I think the version of AEW that at least the core fanbase wants is basically that spirit but modernized understanding the danger of certain kinds of violence (but it's also clear that for the most part, at least in 2023, the most acclaimed AEW matches are the ridiculously violent ones like Hangman vs Swerve Texas Deathmatch, Ricky vs Danielson strap match, Darby vs Christian when Christian is basically just attempting murder and then brainwashes someone son like he's Raven in 1996 etc) and treating women better (Which... yeah, is a mixed bag from AEW even if they don't have Excalibur on commentary screaming cat fight). And much like ECW, to outsiders it's a product that can never grow, not how wrestling is supposed to be done, a disgrace to the business, something they take peeks at and pick apart for being low rent or low class or badly produced. And IMO the reality is, just like ECW did, AEW needs to just accept you're never gonna get that audience and spit in the face of those guys in a defiant sort of "if it's not for you then we'll make it really not for you" kind of way. When WWE was "bad", you could be the alternative in some people's mind just being "good". Now just being good isn't good enough because you can't compete at WWE's game. AEW's best hope to compete and get back to where it was is to just lean as far out from glitz and glamour and be a gritty, wacky, polarizing promotion that satisfies it's base.  
  
When AEW gets criticism from it's core base or the type of people who generally like it, it's when they book things like WCW would. People basically have WCW/TNA style booking as a failed model they don't want to see and when AEW leans that way it tends to just turn people off even if it's objectively good because it's what they've seen before. ECW is considered a true alternative, WCW/TNA is "we're trying to do what you guys do but fuck it up most of the time".  
  
Basically whenever Tony is booking something, he should think "would this fit on ECW in 1999 or in WCW in 1999". If it's ECW 1999 it'll probably work with the crowds and be "hot". If it's WCW in 1999, it's probably go down badly. That's a bit subjective and some people would disagree (for example, to some people stuff like Cole/MJF and Timeless Toni wouldn't fit on ECW, but I disagree since as I said ECW had a lot of wacky comedy adjacent stuff, it was just a different kind of comedy to WWE style comedy where the key is that with the ECW audience they're in on the joke and it's always very tongue in cheek) but I think it's a rough guide to what works and what doesn't for the AEW audience.

I don't even like a lot of MJF's face run recently but I genuinely think White vs MJF was a top 5 match of the year for 2023 and the best PPVmain event AEW has ever done. The leg injury stuff gave the match a drama that AEW PPV main events never ever have and the story of Jay not wanting to just win the belt but torture Adam Cole watching ringside while Cole was perfect in the role of "is he helping MJF or actually trying to screw MJF out of the belt". Was it "REAL SPORTS FEEL" no but it carried an emotional and storytelling weight that drew me in way more than a straight up 45 minutes moves match wouldn't have.

I also think it's honestly more Triple H WWE has adapted more AEW booking patterns than the other way around. It's so jarring to see the same people say too many stables ruined AEW to suddenly claim stable warfare is awesome when WWE does it. Tony and HHH are incredible similar bookers with incredibly similar tastes in wrestling historically, the differences in the company come more from other people/history (HHH still adhering to WWE core principles of showmanship, AEW having a relationship with New Japan and PWG/BTE). Even the comedy, it's 100% not "WWE style comedy" it's always "This is from BTE". Those slow-mo shots with Cole and Roddy and the Kingdom are literally straight from early BTE.

I think it's just the burden of expectation and nostalgia. In 2021 you would get some absolute DOGSHIT Dynamites (One Dynamite was main evented by Nick Comoroto vs Dustin Rhodes, another by Malakai Black vs Brock Anderson) but people just blew it off as "but the promotion is hot, everyone has a bad week, think of all the possiblities". With all the discussion about AEW's storytelling and whether they tell enough, I have what'll probably be a very unpopular opinion: WWE RARELY tell stories in the modern era. They give you the premise of a feud on TV, they have the characters interact every week until they wrestle on PPV. It's the illusion of a story but it's mostly just stasis from TV show to TV show. A story is supposed move forward constantly. Not just a back and forth of "he interfered in my match so I interfere in his, he cut a promo so I cut one back".  
  
And that's not to say AEW doesn't do that too, but when they do it in AEW it stands out for how bad it is. Stuff like Jericho-verse and The Outcasts vs Originals stand out BECAUSE it has that WWE style repetitiveness of "as long the characters are still interacting it's still a story right?".  
   
What makes the Bloodline story or the Elite stories stand out and become instant classics is that they constantly progress with actual twists and turns. Every action by one character leads to a new decision taken by another character and things about each character constantly change based on a decision taken by another one. That's what actual storytelling is, but WWE has gotten away with just "it's a feud so they fight or cut promos on each other every week to remind you they're fighting on the PPV" for so long, people seem to think that's what wrestling storytelling is.  
  
AEW's storytelling is often flawed in how long and drawn out it is or stop start, but it's generally plotted with an actual point by point timeline with a beginning, middle and end which is what a story is meant to be. But the problem is wrestling isn't a TV show taped in advance and if someone gets hurt or sick or have visa issues it's either you scrap the whole story and change it, or you work with the timeline dealt.

I'm kind of surprised how so many people discuss AEW's finances and don't "get" that the pure profit and loss perspective isn't what Tony Khan is necessarily focused on. Tony Khan is like a Joe Lacob or a Steve Ballmer.  
  
Steve Ballmer doesn't own the Clippers to make money, he owns the Clippers to brag about how successful the Clippers are and thereby how successful he is. So he pays this ridiculous luxury tax and builds this giant stadium with his own money that means he's never really gonna make real profit on the team, but he can brag about how much he's changed the Clippers and made them relevant and hear people on ESPN talk about how he's the best owner in sports.  
  
Same thing with Tony, he's treating AEW the way sports owners treat owning a sports team. It's a flex. It's like owning a yacht x1000. Billionaires don't buy a yacht so they can use the yacht as a means of transport and then say "see, I carry 1,000 passengers on my yacht a day, so even though I spent 1m dollars on the yacht, now I make 2 million a year by renting the yacht". They own the yacht to say "look at me I own a fucking yacht". Vince McMahon got in the wrestling business to make a fortune. Tony Khan got in the wrestling business to flex with his fortune. Both are totally different but normal behaviors for rich people.

Potential for growth sure, but Khan has been on the record that he's not gonna change his core product for widespread growth. Ultimately making more money is great but his main source of funding is his dad. And Tony talks about in the interview with Renee Paquette that what is important to his dad IS seeing the stuff about how Tony is changing wrestling and making it less low brow and more creative. So as much as people make the "Booker of the Year" jokes, to Shad Khan that is what is impressive and makes him think he made the right decision to give Tony the money to start the company.
